hypothesis: The aqueous-phase metabolite feature with molecular formula C13H26N5O12S is increased or characteristic in 12-month-old infants fed meat-based complementary protein relative to dairy-based complementary protein.
rationale: Searches for the molecular formula itself ("C13H26N5O12S", formula + HMDB/compound database queries) returned no chemical database entry, no named compound, and no publication reporting this exact elemental composition in any biological matrix, let alone in infant stool/plasma metabolomics. The feature is an unannotated formula-only mass-spectrometry feature (no structure, no external ID), so no direct literature on this feature can exist. What the searches did locate is relevant contextual literature on the exact exposure contrast: the Denver/Colorado randomized controlled feeding trial of formula-fed U.S. infants given meat- vs. dairy-based complementary foods from 5 to 12 months, which reported diet-group differences in serum metabolomics (higher essential and branched-chain amino acids and related nitrogenous derivatives with the higher-protein meat diet) and in fecal microbiome/metabolome features, plus a companion network-learning preprint on the same trial's fecal metabolomics. These establish that meat- vs. dairy-based complementary protein does shift the infant nitrogen- and sulfur-amino-acid-derived metabolite pool, which makes an increase in some nitrogen-rich, sulfur-containing feature at 12 months biologically plausible (meat supplies high loads of purines/nucleotides, methionine, cysteine and taurine, potential precursors of N-rich and sulfated/sulfonated products). However, this is purely generic, pathway-level reasoning: nothing ties the specific composition C13H26N5O12S to the meat group in any direction, and with N5 + O12 + S the formula is compatible with multiple unrelated chemical classes (e.g., a nucleotide/nucleoside-sugar-sulfate conjugate, an aminoglycoside-like or sulfamated amino-sugar, or a peptide-adduct artifact), some of which would be dietary or exogenous rather than microbially derived. Per the rubric this is Weak (1): relevant exposure-level literature but no study of this feature+group combination and no directional evidence.

evidence.title: Different Blood Metabolomics Profiles in Infants Consuming a Meat- or Dairy-Based Complementary Diet
evidence.study_population: U.S. formula-fed term infants in a controlled feeding trial, meat- vs. dairy-based complementary diet from 5 to 12 months, follow-up at 24 months (serum targeted + untargeted metabolomics)
evidence.relevance: Directly addresses the meat vs. dairy complementary-protein contrast at the 12-month timepoint and shows the diet groups differ in circulating amino-acid and nitrogen-containing metabolite profiles (higher essential amino acids with the higher-protein meat diet). Provides exposure-level/pathway plausibility that nitrogen- and sulfur-amino-acid-derived species could be elevated in the meat group, but does not report any compound with formula C13H26N5O12S.

evidence.title: Different gut microbiota in U.S. formula-fed infants consuming a meat vs. dairy-based complementary foods: A randomized controlled trial
evidence.study_population: Full-term formula-fed U.S. infants (Denver metro area) randomized to meat- or dairy-based complementary foods, 5-12 months; fecal microbiota and fecal SCFA
evidence.relevance: Confirms that the specified group contrast produces measurable gut microbial and fecal metabolite (SCFA) differences by 12 months, supporting that diet-driven fecal metabolite features are expected in this design; however it reports no untargeted formula-level features and nothing corresponding to C13H26N5O12S.

evidence.title: Network-based representation learning reveals the impact of age and diet on the gut microbial and metabolomic environment of U.S. infants in a randomized controlled feeding trial
evidence.study_population: 64 exclusively formula-fed 5-month-old U.S. infants randomized to pureed meat (n=32) or dairy foods (n=32) for 7 months; fecal metagenomics and metabolomics
evidence.relevance: Preprint on the same meat-vs-dairy trial analyzing fecal untargeted metabolomics alongside metagenomics; establishes that diet-associated fecal metabolite features are detectable in this exact group comparison, but no evidence was found in the retrieved text that the formula C13H26N5O12S is among the meat-associated features.

caveats: The feature is identified only by an elemental composition (C13H26N5O12S) from aqueous-phase untargeted metabolomics, with no structure, name, HMDB/KEGG/PubChem ID, adduct or retention-time information; searches on a bare molecular formula are intrinsically low-yield and cannot rule out that the underlying compound is well studied under a name we could not infer. Formula-only features are also vulnerable to misassignment (adduct/in-source fragment/isotope artifacts, or in-silico formula ambiguity), and an N5/O12/S composition spans several unrelated chemical classes. Structural annotation (MS/MS spectral matching, or at minimum candidate-formula database lookup) is required before this hypothesis can be meaningfully scored; the score of 1 reflects absence of feature-specific literature, not evidence against the hypothesis.
